chunks: And with this chain he narrated that the Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him) said:

Men are of three types: an intelligent one, a foolish one, and a corrupt one. As for the intelligent one, religion is his law, forbearance is his nature, and judgment is his character. If questioned, he answers; if he speaks, he is correct; if he hears, he understands; if he narrates, he is truthful; and if someone trusts him, he fulfills that trust. As for the foolish one, if invited to good, he neglects it; if invited away from good, he descends into it; if burdened with ignorance, he is ignorant; and if he narrates, he lies. He does not understand, and even if he understands, he does not gain deep insight. As for the corrupt one, if you entrust him with something, he betrays you; if you keep him as a companion, he debases you; and if you trust him, he does not advise you sincerely.

key_terms.أَحْمَق: Foolish person, lacking deep understanding and consistency
key_terms.عَاقِل: Intelligent person, characterized by piety and sound reasoning
key_terms.فَاجِر: Corrupt person, characterized by treachery and insincerity
key_terms.لَا يَتَفَقَّهُ: He does not gain deep insight/understanding

ai.seo_question: What are the three types of men described in Shia hadith and how do they differ in character?
ai.summary: In *Al-Khisal*, Shaykh al-Saduq presents this tripartite classification as a foundational ethical typology, where the 'intelligent' man embodies the integration of divine law (*Shari'ah*) with innate character (*Sijill*), reflecting the Shia ideal of the *Aqil* who harmonizes intellect and piety. The 'foolish' and 'corrupt' types serve as cautionary archetypes, illustrating how a lack of deep comprehension (*Fiqh*) leads to inconsistency, while moral decay results in betrayal (*Khayanah*) even when trusted. This hadith underscores the Shia emphasis on internalizing faith through both cognitive understanding and behavioral integrity.
